newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: From pants to plants, trade tussles teem for WTO.
newsitem.headline: From pants to plants, trade tussles teem for WTO.

text.p: Disputes in the World Trade Organisation (WTO) are mushrooming, involving everything from Costa Rican underwear to Mexican chilled tomatoes, officials said on Tuesday.
"They're increasing in number," Richard Blackhurst, WTO director of economics and research, told Reuters in an interview. "Some of them are also quite important."
Some 62 trade disputes have been filed with the WTO settlement panel at its headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, since its formation after the Uruguay Round trade agreement.
They include a multi-billion dollar battle between Japan and the United States over photographic film and paper involving Eastman Kodak and Fuji Photo Film Co Ltd.

The latest potential dispute would pit the United States, Canada and Russia on one side and the European Union on the other over plans by the EU to impose an import ban on fur from animals caught in leg-hold traps.
EU environment ministers on Monday said they want to lay down tough standards over traps to kill or catch 18 species of wild animals, including muskrats, beavers, sables, lynx and wolves.
Most of the problems, however, do not have such a high profile.
They also include what may be considered mundane issues such as the Costa Rican protest against U.S. restrictions on its underwear exports.
Washington was also accused by Mexico of violating WTO rules by initiating an anti-dumping probe in the imporation of Mexican fresh and chilled tomatoes.
The Philippines has filed a complaint against Brazil over duties on exports of its dessicated coconuts.
The products involved, however, cannot be dismissed too lightly.

In the Philippines, for instance, coconut farming is a major industry employing up to five million of the country's 70 million people and is its leading agricultural export. Coconut oil sales in 1995 reached an all-time high of over $1.0 billion.
Blackhurst said he is encouraged by the number of disputes beginning to reach the WTO.

"It shows confidence in the dispute settlement system," he said. "Previously, one country could block the process at any stage. It took a consensus to go ahead. Now, that's turned completely on its head. It takes a consensus not to go ahead."
A European diplomat added: "That's what you have the WTO for, to take care of all these disputes over trade."
The problem facing poor countries in bringing their disputes to the WTO is that most cannot afford to permanently assign staff in Geneva to handle their cases.
Blackhurst said major economic powers such as the United States, Japan and the EU can easily have more than 10 full-time staff working on trade issues alone in Geneva.
Poorer nations often have to make do with about two people who have to handle all international organisations headquartered in Switzerland, not just the WTO, he added.
But most countries feel there is no alternative to the current system and believe bringing disputes to the WTO for resolution is better than nothing.
"If...no one gives in, it can be most disconcerting," Philippine Trade and Industry Secretary Cesar Bautista told reporters.
